extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetry, aesthetics, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for judging works of poetry and fine art from an Aristotelian/critical perspective — what counts as the proper end of art, how to judge artistic merit, and the relation of poetry to morality and audience. Useful for literary critics, teachers, and advanced creative-writing students.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of art is subjective pleasure in the percipient
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of art is in its nature an appeal to the senses and imagination of the person to whom it is presented; its perfection and success depend on a subjective impression. It attains to complete existence only within the mind, in the pleasure which accompanies this mode of mental activity (ἐνέργεια).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art's productive activity is subordinated to the receptive activity of the person for whom it is produced; the artist's aim is the pleasure experienced by the percipient rather than any external property of the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's subjective emotion has objective validity via human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective emotion evoked by art is deeply grounded in human nature, and thence acquires a kind of objective validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although effect is subjective, it must be a response rooted in 'normal human sympathies and faculties' to count as the proper end of art; the universal element in responses legitimizes aesthetic judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: The ideal/cultivated spectator is the standard of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The final appeal is made to a man of sound aesthetic instincts (ὁ ψυχὴς), who is the standard of taste; he is no mere expert and Aristotle prefers the popular judgment — but of a cultivated public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment should be sought from a free and educated listener rather than vulgar specialists; this ideal spectator represents the rule and standard for the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish higher and lower kinds of audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Both in the Politics and in the Poetics Aristotle distinguishes between the lower and the higher kind of audience. The ‘free and educated listener’ at a musical performance is opposed to one of the vulgar sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different classes of audience enjoy different kinds of music/poetry; inferior enjoyment is permitted when that is the audience's capacity, but the art's aim addresses the cultivated spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: The end of any art is the pleasure distinctive to that art
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of any art is not ‘any chance pleasure’, but the pleasure which is distinctive of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should aim to produce the characteristic pleasure (e.g., the tragic pleasure of pity and fear in tragedy) rather than incidental or irrelevant gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must awaken pity and fear (its distinctive function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic action has an inherent capacity of calling forth pity and fear; this quality must be impressed by the poet on the dramatic material; the test of artistic merit in a tragedy is the degree in which it fulfils this, its distinctive function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All rules for tragic construction (plot, character, recognition, catastrophe) flow from the requirement to produce the union of the pitiable and the terrible that yields tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of structure derive from primary aesthetic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All the rules prescribed for the tragic poet flow from the same primary requirement — those which determine the proper construction of the plot, the character of the ideal hero, the best form of recognition and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal elements (unity, sequence, recognition, construction) are justified instrumentally by their service to the art's distinctive effect; evaluate structural choices by how well they realize that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry judged by its own laws, not by external (moral/scientific) standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of correctness in poetry and politics is not the same, any more than in poetry and any other art. Poetry is not a metrical version of the facts of medicine, physics, or history. It must be judged by its own laws, its own fundamental assumptions, and not by an alien standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate poetic truth by scientific or political truth; assess within the conventions and aims of the poetic form under consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should represent the general, not the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Art ought to represent the general not the particular; personal satire is ranked as an inferior type of art because it focuses on the particular rather than the general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer representations that exemplify general human types and conditions (typical characters, universal situations) over mere individual attack or isolated anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of vice is only excused by necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of moral depravity finds its only excuse in 'necessity.' The necessity meant is the inner necessity arising out of the structure of a piece. Gratuitous wickedness is forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vice may appear on stage only if demanded by the cogent necessity of dramatic motive (e.g., to enable contrasted character or to drive the plot); avoid gratuitous or unmotivated wickedness — example cited: Menelaus in Euripides' Orestes as gratuitous wickedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge moral influence in context (do not isolate parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech or action must be interpreted in the light of all the circumstances — the persons, the occasion, the end it is designed to serve. The moral influence of a poem should be judged by a similar rule of criticism. The effect resides not in the isolated parts but in the scheme of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing alleged moral harm, consider the whole artistic scheme and dramatic context rather than isolated lines or episodes; avoid condemning authors for passages removed from their setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be appropriate to their aesthetic role (σπουδαῖοι/φαῦλοι distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad distinction is drawn between the imitative arts, according as they represent persons morally noble (σπουδαίους) or ignoble (φαύλους), or of an intermediate type resembling average humanity (ὁμοίους). Comedy aims at representing men as worse, tragedy as better than in actual life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose character-types (noble/idealized for tragedy, inferior/worse for comedy) to suit the genre's aim; 'σπουδαῖος' in tragic contexts carries a moral/ethical sense tied to the aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral content/author's character matter only insofar as they affect the total impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Not that Aristotle would set aside as a matter of indifference the moral content of a poem or the moral character of the author. Nay, they are all-important factors in producing the total impression which has to be made upon the hearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While aesthetic and formal criteria are primary, consider moral matter and authorship insofar as they contribute to or detract from the unity and effectiveness of the artistic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's educational/didactic use is secondary for mature audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of poetry, as of all the fine arts, is to produce an emotional delight, a pure and elevated pleasure. The didactic point of view is abandoned in critical analysis: for the grown man the poet's function is not that of a teacher, or if a teacher he is only so by accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between poetry's capacity to instruct (useful in youth or civic education) and its primary aesthetic purpose for adult audiences; do not evaluate adult poetic art solely by its didactic utility.
